newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan poll shows China strangling Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan poll shows China strangling Hong Kong.

text.p: People on Taiwan believe China's communist government will strangle Hong Kong's freedom and prosperity in a pattern that many fear eventually will extend to their own island, a poll published on Thursday showed.

The survey, conducted by the mass-circulation United Daily News, showed that 54 percent of 1,189 respondents said Hong Kong would not be able to maintain its "free life" after reverting to Beijing's control in mid-1997.

Only 23 percent said China would not interfere with life in Hong Kong -- echoing the scepticism of Taiwan's leaders on China's "one country, two systems" vow to let Hong Kong run itself autonomously for 50 years after reunification.
Beijing often touts the "one country, two systems" model for Taiwan's own eventual reunification with the mainland.
Some 42 percent believed Hong Kong would not sustain economic prosperity under communist authority, while only 32 percent said the territory's booming capitalism would continue.

The survey indicated Taiwan still distrusts China and that Beijing's handling of Hong Kong's handover has made Taiwanese wary of their own future in view of China's vow to "return Taiwan to the motherland".

Taiwan and China were split by a civil war that ended in 1949. Beijing regards Taiwan as a renegade province and threatens to attack if it strays from its avowed goal of reunification and tries to pursue independence instead.

A scant 19 percent of Taiwan people polled said they wished to reunify with China while just 21 percent support declaration of formal independence. Far more, 45 percent, would like to to keep things the way they are -- de facto independence.

When asked what actually would happen to Taiwan rather than what they wished would happen, 23 percent said they expected the island to reunify with China while only 11 percent expected it to achieve independence.
Only 37 percent expect things to stay unchanged.

Taipei espouses eventual reunification but insists that its exiled Republic of China government already enjoys sovereignty over Taiwan -- a declaration China suspects is an endorsement of the island's independence.
China launched war games near Taiwan in the months leading up to the island's March presidential election to dissuade voters from supporting pro-independence candidates.
The electorate gave incumbent Lee Teng-hui -- the primary target of China's intimidation -- a landslide victory that made him the first directly elected leader in Chinese history.
Taipei says it cannot consider reunification until China adopts democratic reforms like those in Taiwan itself.
It flatly rejects Beijing's offer of unification under the one country, two systems model.
Taiwan leaders voice doubt that Beijing's communist leaders can keep their hands off Hong Kong as promised.

On December 12, a Beijing-appointed panel selected shipping mogul Tung Chee-hwa to take over as Hong Kong's chief executive from July 1, saying this was the birth of true democracy after 150 years of British colonial control.
Chinese officials have said the Hong Kong handover should reassure Taiwan that China is earnest in its pledge to allow the island to keep its political system under Beijing's rule.
